findings.what: Uniform resampling blur across the whole window: the mosaic is presented at 1 px = 0.1725 ft but carries only about half that much real detail, so every rule is a soft grey ramp instead of a crisp line. Evidence: (a) a 2x downsample/upsample round trip changes the image by only 0.94 RMS (max 18/255) - i.e. there is essentially no image content above half-Nyquist; the radial power spectrum has already fallen ~3 orders of magnitude by 0.15 Nyquist; (b) the paper-to-ink transition on the wharf bulkhead line takes 4-5 px (185 -> 30) where a native-resolution scan takes 1-2, peak gradient only ~40/px against a step's ~77; (c) the hairline rail rules in the yard measure 6-8 px FWHM (1.0-1.4 ft) and bottom out at only 68-84 grey, never reaching full ink density - the classic signature of a stroke finer than the effective point-spread. This is not the JPEG: the window's own luma quantisation table starts 4,3,2 (~q90) and 8-px block-boundary contrast is only 1.28x interior, so the softness is in the underlying mosaic, not the QC export. Practical effect in print: the smallest hand lettering ('CARPR. SHOP', the '(1.R.CL.)' annotation at ~0.07,0.77) sits right at the edge of legibility. NOTE: this is uniform over the entire window - the per-100px max-gradient map is a flat 35-46 wherever there is linework, with no locally smeared patch - so it is almost certainly a global property of the mosaic build rather than anything specific to this tile. It should be deduplicated across windows, not counted 33 times.

(2) Shearing the image by the tracked slope (0.267) and profiling six x-bands shows the bulkhead pinned at y=463-464 in every band and all four rails plus both strands of the dashed line present in every band, drifting smoothly by a consistent 26 px over the full width (their true slope is 0.250, slightly off the bulkhead's) - no line steps, doubles, breaks or disappears. So: map content in this window is clean. The single finding above is a global image-quality property of the mosaic, not a map error, and I have flagged it as such rather than as a defect in this tile.

Refuted. The bright top region is a lighter, cleaner plate's paper, not unpainted canvas, and the numbers the finding rests on do not hold up.

1) The "no paper grain at all, std 1.7 vs std 20+ for genuine plate regions" comparison is wrong. Measured on blank paper (no ink) in this same window: the bright band at x850-1250/y40-200 gives per-channel std 3.0/2.8/2.6 and high-frequency (grain) std 0.47; the band at x480-760/y150-250 gives 3.2/3.3/3.6, hf 0.53. Accepted warm paper measured the same way gives std 4.1/4.6/6.7, hf 0.63 (x100-350, y700-900) and 3.6/3.9/3.7, hf 0.74 (x950-1250, y400-560). That is the same order of grain, not "none versus plenty." The only patch in this window that actually reaches std ~22 is x1150-1350/y1250-1450, and it reaches it because a black street rule runs through it — that is ink, not grain. The reviewer's "std 20+" baseline is measuring ink and foxing mottle, both of which the brief explicitly excludes.

2) It is not a flat fill. Along y=30 the band runs smoothly from RGB(174,166,155) at x=0 to (149,145,136) at x=1400 — a scanner illumination falloff. A canvas fill would be one constant value.

3) It is not blank canvas, because the same cool-gray sheet carries ink all over this window. Reading the gray as canvas would require canvas to hold printing. On it: the house-number row "17 2519 2521" with its block-face rule at about (0.07-0.20, 0.13-0.16); the large plate-index "3" glyph and the vertical street rule at x≈0.28, y 0.12-0.40; the lot number "3302" at (0.31, 0.20); the street-width numeral "70'" at (0.42, 0.19); and the pair of diagonal street rules crossing the band at (0.88-0.95, 0.0-0.17), which are drawn continuously across the gray at full ink density.

4) What is left over is exactly what the brief says to ignore: a paper-tone step between two plates (the cool sheet is R-B ≈ 16, the warm neighbour R-B ≈ 45) along an irregular seam polygon. The genuinely empty parts of it — roughly x 0.55-0.87, y 0-0.16 — are about 86 x 40 ft at this 0.1725 ft/px scale, i.e. ordinary Sanborn blank roadway and yard space between the numbered block faces, which is what a 70-ft street flanked by lot numbers looks like when nothing is built on it.

Separately, and not part of this finding: the left rule of the diagonal street near (0.9, 0.03) sits at a different offset above and below the seam, so the two plates draw that street at different widths. The brief names that as a 1912 source disagreement and not a defect, so I am not raising it either.

Could not refute. Two large bold display letters of the street-name label (readable as C and G/O when rotated upright) are cut flat mid-stroke along that edge: the ink terminates on an exactly vertical line at x=446-450 continuously from y=165 to y=275, 110px of straight-cut ink against a ~30px stroke weight. Right of the cut the tile supplies only blank paper plus a single 70' width numeral at (0.42,0.20) - the label's missing halves are never redrawn, so the street name is unreadable at that spot. This is not excluded as paper tone, hand lettering, an adjoining-sheet numeral, or a street-width disagreement (both plates read 70'); a street label guillotined by a rectangular blank patch would be wrong in a printed map. Severity sits at the high end of minor given how prominent the display lettering is.
